summary: No. With both estimators at scikit-learn defaults inside an identical preprocessing pipeline (median/mode imputation, standardized numerics, one-hot categoricals), logistic regression very slightly outperforms the random forest on stratified 5-fold CV ROC-AUC: 0.9056 vs 0.9010, a difference of -0.0045 in favor of LogReg. The gap is tiny in absolute terms (~0.4% AUC) but highly consistent across folds and seeds. Important caveat: this conclusion is contingent on standardizing the numeric features -- without scaling, default LogisticRegression (lbfgs, max_iter=100) fails to converge and RF wins by a large margin.
direction: LogReg > RF (RF does NOT outperform; difference is small but consistent)
methodological_choices: Both models wrapped in the SAME sklearn Pipeline so the estimator is the only difference, with all preprocessing fit inside each CV fold (no leakage). Missing values ('?' in workclass/occupation/native-country, ~5.7% of rows) imputed rather than dropped: median for numerics, most-frequent for categoricals. Numeric features standardized with StandardScaler -- this is the single most consequential choice, since it is what lets default LogisticRegression (lbfgs, max_iter=100) converge; scaling is a no-op for RF. Categoricals one-hot encoded with handle_unknown='ignore' (~105 columns; native-country has 41 levels). All 14 features kept including fnlwgt, a census sampling weight that arguably is not a legitimate predictor. Target binarized as >50K = 1 (23.9% positive). Estimators left at library defaults exactly as specified (RF: 100 trees, unlimited depth; LogReg: L2, C=1.0, lbfgs); RF given random_state=0 for reproducibility, n_jobs=-1 for speed. Metric: roc_auc_score on predict_proba; class imbalance left unhandled (no class_weight, no resampling), which is defensible since ROC-AUC is threshold-free and insensitive to base rate. Comparison is paired -- both models scored on identical fold splits, so per-fold differences are directly comparable. Another researcher could reasonably have (a) skipped scaling, (b) dropped rows with missing values, (c) used ordinal/target encoding for the 41-level country variable, or (d) dropped fnlwgt -- see verification_result for how much each of these moves the answer.
verification_method: Three independent checks: (1) 5x repeated stratified 5-fold CV with seeds 0-4 (25 distinct folds), summarized with a normal-approximation 95% CI and a 10,000-resample percentile bootstrap over the fold-level paired differences; (2) a fresh 80/20 stratified train/test split (seed 123) not used in the CV analysis, models refit on the 80% and scored once on the held-out 20%; (3) sensitivity re-runs perturbing the three most debatable preprocessing choices -- no numeric scaling, LogReg max_iter raised to 2000, and fnlwgt removed.
verification_result: The finding held up, and the effect is if anything slightly smaller than the initial estimate. Repeated CV (25 folds): LogReg 0.90537 vs RF 0.90175, mean difference -0.00361 with 95% CI [-0.00443, -0.00280] (bootstrap CI [-0.00440, -0.00281]) -- the interval excludes zero, and RF won only 1 of 25 folds. The untouched 80/20 holdout agreed in sign and magnitude: LogReg 0.90378 vs RF 0.90116, difference -0.00262. Revised estimate: RF - LogReg = -0.0036, 95% CI [-0.0044, -0.0028]. Sensitivity runs: raising LogReg max_iter to 2000 changed nothing (-0.00452, identical to default), so the result is not a convergence artifact. Dropping fnlwgt widened the gap in LogReg's favor (-0.0159; RF fell to 0.8895 while LogReg was unchanged), meaning RF derives real signal from what is only a survey sampling weight -- so the headline result is conservative toward RF. The one choice that flips the conclusion is scaling: with unscaled numerics, default LogReg scores only 0.594 and RF wins by +0.307; even allowing unscaled LogReg to converge (max_iter=1000) it reaches just 0.882 and RF wins by +0.019. So a researcher who applied LogisticRegression() to unstandardized features would have reached the opposite conclusion, and that fork -- not the estimators themselves -- is what determines the answer to H2.
